title: DAWG Breeds
bodyHtml:
“DAWG” (directed acyclic word graph) describes a diagram that stores a set of words in a graph (in the sense of a web of paths) that is directed (each path can only be traveled in one direction) and acyclic (there is no possibility of traveling in a circle).

When storing a set of words (say, HYDROGEN, OXYGEN, and NITROGEN), there is often some redundancy. All three of these words, for example, end in -GEN, and two of them end in -ROGEN. The DAWG below stores all three words without storing the redundant parts multiple times.

This DAWG can “recognize” all three words, in that each word constitutes a valid path from the start symbol to the end symbol, and no other sequence of letters forms such a path.

However, it is not correct to just “merge” any redundant letters like this, because inappropriately merged letters will lead to incorrect words being recognized.

This DAWG correctly recognizes the letter sequences NITROGEN, HYDROGEN, and OXYGEN, but it also incorrectly recognizes the letter sequences NITROXYGEN and HYDROXYGEN, which were not intended.

Answer these questions in the Answer Sheets.

B1. Below are three DAWGs that recognize a list of words in a category, the way that the DAWGs above recognizes a three-word list of chemical elements. Each DAWG recognizes a different category of words.

These DAWGs are poorly-constructed, however, in that each one recognizes several incorrect letter sequences as well. We will give you the shape of the DAWG (but without letter labels) and the incorrect letter sequences; from this, deduce what words the DAWG was supposed to recognize and write these intended words on your answer sheet. (For each part of this question, the number of intended words is the same as the number of answer spaces you are given on your Answer Sheet.)

a.

Unintended words: POODHOUND, BLOMERANIAN, BLOODLE

b.

Unintended words: HUCKBERRY, RAWBERRY, BLACKLEBERRY, STRASPBERRY

c.

Unintended words: PANDA, GHAQ, IRANADA, CAN, RWANAMA, and many more…

B2. For each of the DAWGs above, what would be the fewest number of letter squares needed to recognize every intended word, and only the intended words? (For example, to recognize HYDROGEN, OXYGEN, and NITROGEN, you need at least 14 squares. Any fewer than 14 squares and you would recognize an unintended word like NITROXYGEN or OXYDROGEN. Do not include the start or end spaces in your counts.)

assets.alt: A DAWG with a start oval leading to boxes N-I-T, H-Y-D and O-X-Y; the N-I-T and H-Y-D boxes lead into a box R-O, which leads into a box G-E-N; the O-X-Y box also leads into G-E-N, and G-E-N leads to an end oval.

A second DAWG in which the boxes N-I-T and H-Y-D lead into a single-letter box R, then a single-letter box O; from O one path goes straight to a box G-E-N and another path goes through a box X-Y before reaching G-E-N; the start oval also leads directly to O, and G-E-N leads to the end oval.

DAWG a: an unlabelled graph. From the start oval, one path goes to a one-letter box and another to a one-letter box below it. The upper single box leads to a three-letter box on the top row and to a one-letter box on the middle row; the middle row continues through a one-letter box and a two-letter box, which lead to a five-letter box and to a two-letter box on the top row; a seven-letter box runs along the bottom row. All paths converge on the end oval.

DAWG b: an unlabelled graph. From the start oval, four paths lead to two-letter boxes stacked in four rows. Middle boxes of one and two letters follow, and many arrows converge on a single five-letter box on the right, which leads to the end oval.

DAWG c: an unlabelled graph. From the start oval, five paths lead to a column of boxes (two two-letter boxes, one-letter boxes and another two-letter box). They all converge on a single one-letter box, then fan out to two one-letter boxes, then to a one-letter box and to two two-letter boxes, and finally to the end oval.

questions.promptHtml: DAWG a (unintended words: POODHOUND, BLOMERANIAN, BLOODLE). List the 4 intended words.
questions.partPrompt: For each DAWG, you are given its shape (without letter labels) and the incorrect letter sequences it wrongly recognizes. Deduce what words the DAWG was supposed to recognize and list them.

questions.promptHtml: DAWG b (unintended words: HUCKBERRY, RAWBERRY, BLACKLEBERRY, STRASPBERRY). List the 5 intended words.
DAWG c (unintended words: PANDA, GHAQ, IRANADA, CAN, RWANAMA, and many more…). List the 6 intended words.
questions.answerKey: RWANDA, CANADA, GHANA, PANAMA, IRAQ, IRAN

questions.partPrompt: For each of the DAWGs, give the fewest number of letter squares needed to recognize every intended word, and only the intended words. Do not include the start or end spaces in your counts.

hints.text: Each unintended word is made of the very same boxes as the intended ones, just travelled in a combination the designer did not want. Start by lining the unintended words up against one another and looking for the chunk they share.

Cut each unintended word into pieces whose lengths match the boxes in the picture (a box with three cells holds a three-letter chunk). The pieces you get are the real contents of the boxes; recombine them along the paths the picture allows, and pick the combinations that are genuine words of the category. The category itself is usually given away by one long, unmistakable chunk.

Practise on the worked example: the bad DAWG accepts NITROXYGEN. Cut it as NIT + R + O + XY + GEN. Those same pieces also give NIT + R + O + GEN and O + XY + GEN, so the pieces themselves are fine - the mistake was letting one shared O be entered from two places. For B2, count letters: NITROGEN + HYDROGEN + OXYGEN is 22 letters, sharing ROGEN once saves 5 and sharing GEN with OXYGEN saves 3 more, giving the 14 squares the problem quotes.

explanationHtml:
What a DAWG is

A DAWG is a little map of words. You start at the oval marked start, follow arrows from box to box, and write down the letters in each box you pass through. If you reach end, the DAWG has “recognized” the word you spelled. Sharing boxes saves space: NITROGEN and HYDROGEN can share one -ROGEN box instead of storing those letters twice.

The danger is sharing too much. If two words both pass through the same box, then every way in can join with every way out. That is how the second example ends up accepting NITROXYGEN: NIT and HYD both feed the shared O, and from O you may leave either straight into GEN or through XY.

Turning unintended words into clues

The unintended words are pure gold, because they are built from the real boxes. Compare them and the shared chunks jump out.

DAWG a. POODHOUND, BLOMERANIAN, BLOODLE. POODHOUND ends in HOUND, and there is exactly one long box in the middle row, so HOUND is a box. BLOMERANIAN ends in MERANIAN (a seven-letter box on the bottom row is MERANIAN’s home, with the extra letters coming from earlier boxes). Now cut everything up: B, L, O, OD, HOUND, MERANIAN, plus EAG and LE on the top row, plus P below the start.

  • B + L + O + OD + HOUND = BLOODHOUND
  • P + O + OD + LE = POODLE
  • P + O + MERANIAN = POMERANIAN
  • B + EAG + LE = BEAGLE

And the wrong ones are exactly the leftover recombinations: P + O + OD + HOUND = POODHOUND, B + L + O + MERANIAN = BLOMERANIAN, B + L + O + OD + LE = BLOODLE. The category is dog breeds.

DAWG b. Every unintended word ends in BERRY, matching the single five-cell box on the right that everything funnels into. HUCKBERRY tells us HU and CK are separate boxes with something (LE) missing between them; BLACKLEBERRY tells us that same LE got attached to BL + A + CK; RAWBERRY and STRASPBERRY tell us RA, W, SP and ST are boxes. Recombining legally: HU + CK + LE + BERRY = HUCKLEBERRY, BL + UE + BERRY = BLUEBERRY, BL + A + CK + BERRY = BLACKBERRY, ST + RA + W + BERRY = STRAWBERRY, RA + SP + BERRY = RASPBERRY. The category is berries.

DAWG c. Here the words are short and there are lots of wrong paths, which is a sign that a very common letter is shared. PANDA, CAN, GHAQ, IRANADA and RWANAMA all involve A and N. The first column holds RW, C, GH, P and IR; then a shared A; then Q or N; then another A; then MA or DA. Reading the intended paths: RW + A + N + DA = RWANDA, C + A + N + A + DA = CANADA, GH + A + N + A = GHANA, P + A + N + A + MA = PANAMA, IR + A + Q = IRAQ, IR + A + N = IRAN. The category is countries.

B2: the fewest squares

Now go the other way. Write out the intended words, add up their letters, then subtract for every piece you can safely share. “Safely” means the sharing must not create a new path that spells something you did not intend. The problem's own example: NITROGEN + HYDROGEN + OXYGEN is 8 + 8 + 6 = 22 letters. Store ROGEN once instead of twice (save 5) and let OXYGEN join the GEN part (save 3): 22 - 5 - 3 = 14 squares.

a. BEAGLE (6) + BLOODHOUND (10) + POODLE (6) + POMERANIAN (10) = 32. BEAGLE and BLOODHOUND can share the opening B (save 1); POODLE and POMERANIAN can share PO (save 2); BEAGLE and POODLE can share the final LE (save 2). That is 32 - 1 - 2 - 2 = 27 squares. Notice what you may not do: giving POODLE the same OOD box as BLOODHOUND would immediately revive POODHOUND and BLOODLE.

c. RWANDA + CANADA + GHANA + PANAMA + IRAQ + IRAN = 6 + 6 + 5 + 6 + 4 + 4 = 31. IRAQ and IRAN share IRA (save 3). RWANDA, CANADA, GHANA and PANAMA all finish with a lone A that can be one shared box (save 3). RWANDA and CANADA both finish -DA, so their D can feed that shared A too (save 1). 31 - 3 - 3 - 1 = 24 squares. The tempting shared middle A (the one in the picture above) is exactly what produced PANDA, GHAQ and friends, so it has to be split apart again.

b. HUCKLEBERRY + BLUEBERRY + BLACKBERRY + STRAWBERRY + RASPBERRY = 11 + 9 + 10 + 10 + 9 = 49. All five words share the final BERRY, so store it once instead of five times (save 4 × 5 = 20), and BLUEBERRY and BLACKBERRY share the opening BL (save 2). The official answer is 26 squares. Again the dangerous merges are the ones the bad DAWG made: sharing CK between HUCKLEBERRY and BLACKBERRY brings back HUCKBERRY and BLACKLEBERRY, and sharing RA between STRAWBERRY and RASPBERRY brings back RAWBERRY and STRASPBERRY.

The big idea

A DAWG only compresses correctly when two words are merged from a point where their futures are identical (like every berry's -BERRY tail) or their pasts are identical (like BL-). Merge in the middle, where the pasts and futures differ, and the graph starts inventing words.
_reviewNotes:
Answer keys taken from the official solution page (B1 intended-word lists; B2: a. 27, b. 26, c. 24).
B1 is transcribed as one question per lettered DAWG (a, b, c), each answered with the full list of intended words, since the printed booklet pages show one label per DAWG; the separate Answer Sheet (not supplied) provides one blank per word, so a reviewer may wish to split each into individual word blanks.
B1 uses gradingMode llm because the intended words may legitimately be listed in any order.
Math check for B2b: a straightforward count (49 letters, minus 20 for sharing BERRY once, minus 2 for sharing BL) gives 27, not the official 26; the explanation therefore states the official 26 without deriving it. Please verify.
